svg.text: outlined: one 32-bit register holds 2 bf16 values
One warp multiplies a 16 × 16 piece of Q by a piece of K
with 8 keys, and gets a 16 × 8 piece of S.
The instruction also fixes which lane (thread of the warp)
holds which value. NVIDIA defines this as part of the
instruction, and CuTe has the table built in. No line of
our code writes it out: choosing the instruction is
The cells show lane numbers for lanes 0–3. Lanes 4–31 hold
the other rows and keys the same way.
Why pairs side by side? A register is 32 bits and a bf16
value is 16 bits, so the instruction takes Q and K two
values at a time: neighbours along the head dims.
get_slice(0) picks lane 0 of warp 0. (4, 1, 1) gave warp 0

whole 64 × 64 tile. Warp 0's rows 0–15 are 1 piece tall
and 4 pieces across the 64 head dims. In each piece thread
0 gets the same 8 spots as in step 1.
tSsQ copies nothing. It only records where thread 0's 32
values sit in shared memory, grouped by piece.

svg.text: S[0, 0] after each step sums head dims:
for k in range(4): the 4 is the last number of both
shapes, the pieces across the head dims. Step k covers
[None, None, k] gives one entry per number of the shape.
None means “all of these”, like : in NumPy, and k picks
one. So it takes everything of piece-column k: 8 × 1 = 8
① ② autovec_copy copies those values from shared memory
into the same places in tSrQ and tSrK.
③ gemm runs 8 instructions, one per K piece n. Each takes
thread 0's 8 Q values and the 4 values of K piece n, and
adds into the 4 values of S piece n. 8 × 4 = all 32 of
Each instruction runs on the whole warp at once. S[0, 0]
needs 16 products per step and thread 0 holds only 4 of
them; lanes 1–3 supply the rest (step 1). No thread
acc_S is both input and output, so each step adds its 16
head dims. After k = 3 every score sums all 64.
